claim: Co-culturing AML and stromal cells in direct contact triggers increased acetate secretion compared to cells cultured separately.
source: The most striking difference found in co-culture compared to cells cultured separately was an increased secretion of acetate, which was common for the three cell lines used (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental NMR data showing acetate levels in co-culture vs. separate cultures across multiple AML cell lines.

claim: Only stromal cells secrete acetate when cultured alone, whereas AML cells do not secrete acetate when cultured alone.
source: Moreover, only stromal cells secreted acetate to a lower extent when cultured alone whereas AML cells did not secrete any acetate when cultured alone.
evidence: Supported by NMR measurements of extracellular acetate in separate cultures.

claim: Stromal cells are responsible for the increased acetate secretion found in co-culture.
source: Moreover, only stromal cells secreted acetate to a lower extent when cultured alone whereas AML cells did not secrete any acetate when cultured alone. Altogether, these findings suggest that acetate secretion is a result of a direct interaction between AML and stromal cells. In addition, the observation that only stromal cells secrete acetate under these conditions suggests that stromal cells could be responsible for the increased acetate secretion found in co-culture.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only stromal cells secrete acetate when cultured alone.

claim: Direct cell-to-cell contact is required for increased acetate secretion in co-culture.
source: Co-culturing cells using a permeable membrane blocked the increase in acetate secretion observed under direct contact conditions (Figure 1C). In fact, cells in co-culture presented lower levels of acetate than MS-5 cells cultured alone revealing that direct cell-to-cell contact is required for acetate secretion in co-culture.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing direct contact vs. permeable membrane co-culture conditions.

claim: Increased acetate secretion is specific for AML-stromal cell interaction and not observed with other cancer cell types.
source: We found that there was no acetate secretion in co-culture, also not by HeLa and AML cells cultured alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that increased acetate secretion is specific for an AML-stromal cell interaction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing AML-stromal co-cultures with HeLa-AML co-cultures.

claim: MS-5 stromal cells are responsible for acetate secretion when co-cultured with AML cells.
source: Extracellular acetate levels in previously co-cultured MS-5 cells followed a similar trend as before separation, suggesting that the MS-5 cells most likely are responsible for the increased acetate secretion found in co-culture (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing continued acetate secretion by MS-5 cells after separation from co-culture.

claim: Three out of four primary AML patient samples showed increased acetate levels when co-cultured with MS-5 cells compared to MS-5 cells cultured alone.
source: We found that three out of four primary AML samples presented higher levels of acetate when co-cultured with MS-5 cells compared to MS-5 cells cultured alone (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental NMR data from primary patient samples.

claim: Healthy donor CD34+ cells do not show increased acetate secretion when co-cultured with MS-5 cells.
source: Contrary, none of the healthy donor samples showed an increased acetate secretion in co-culture suggesting that acetate secretion is specific for AML cells in co-culture (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from healthy donor samples.

claim: Mice with MLL-AF9+ leukemia have significantly higher acetate levels in bone marrow extracellular fluid compared to control mice.
source: These experiments revealed that a significantly higher amount of acetate was present in the BMEF of mice suffering from leukaemia compared to controls (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by in vivo NMR measurements of bone marrow extracellular fluid.

claim: The concentration of secreted acetate in co-culture is approximately 3-4 mM.
source: For this, we compared a sample of extracellular medium from a co-culture of SKM-1 and MS-5 cells after 24 hr to a calibration curve (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which allowed us to determine the concentration of acetate in co-culture as approximately 3–4 mM.
evidence: Supported by NMR calibration curve analysis.

claim: SKM-1 cells consume acetate at both normal plasma concentrations (0.25 mM) and co-culture concentrations (3 mM).
source: We then investigated whether SKM-1 cells can consume acetate both in normal plasma concentrations (Gao et al., 2016) and co-culture concentrations (0.25 mM or 3 mM, respectively). In both cases, SKM-1 cells consumed acetate significantly after 48 hr, and in normal plasma conditions also after 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental NMR data showing acetate consumption over time, with citation to Gao et al., 2016 for normal plasma concentrations.

claim: SKM-1 cells, but not MS-5 cells, incorporate 13C label from [2-13C]acetate into TCA cycle metabolites.
source: Both cell types imported 13C labelled acetate as observed in NMR spectra (Figure 2B). However, only SKM-1 cells showed 13C label incorporation in several TCA cycle related metabolites, including aspartate, citrate, glutamate, 2-oxoglutarate, glutathione, and proline, as well as in acetylcarnitine.
evidence: Supported by 1H-13C-HSQC NMR spectroscopy data showing label incorporation patterns.

claim: AML cells in co-culture rapidly incorporate 13C from [2-13C]acetate into TCA cycle metabolites within 30 minutes.
source: We found that only AML cells incorporated 13C into intracellular metabolites at both timepoints (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C). The intake of acetate by AML cells was very rapid, with several TCA cycle metabolites such as glutamate, oxoglutarate, malate, proline, and succinate showing label incorporation after 30 min of [2-13C]acetate labelling.
evidence: Supported by tracer-based NMR experiments with [2-13C]acetate in co-culture.

claim: AML cells incorporate 13C from [2-13C]acetate into lipids after 48 hours but not after 8 hours of labeling.
source: No 13C labelling was incorporated into lipids when co-cultures were labelled with [2-13C]acetate for 8 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). In contrast, at 48 hr the three AML cell lines presented 1H13C-methyl signals at 0.7–0.8 ppm confirming labelling of lipid CH3 groups (approximately 10–20% enrichment) (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by 1H NMR spectroscopy of lipid extracts at different time points.

claim: AML cells can uptake and utilize acetate secreted by stromal cells in co-culture as a substrate to feed the TCA cycle and for lipid biosynthesis.
source: Overall, these results indicated that AML cells could uptake and utilise the acetate secreted by stromal cells in co-culture as a substrate to feed into the TCA cycle and for lipid biosynthesis.
evidence: Supported by multiple tracer-based NMR experiments showing label incorporation from acetate into TCA metabolites and lipids.

claim: HL-60 cells show high sensitivity to AraC that can be partially counteracted by the presence of acetate.
source: Our data showed that the AML cells studied displayed different degrees of sensitivity to AraC, with HL-60 cells being more sensitive and Kasumi-1 more resistant (Figure 2E). Interestingly, we observed that the high sensitivity for AraC displayed by HL-60 cells could be partially counteracted by the presence of acetate in the cultures.
evidence: Supported by cell viability assays with AraC treatment in different media conditions.

claim: All human AML cell lines studied display high sensitivity to ACSS2 inhibitor when cultured in glucose with no added acetate.
source: All human AML cell lines studied displayed high sensitivity to the ACSS2i when cultured in glucose with no added acetate, indicating the importance of ACSS2 in metabolism, as previously observed in myeloma cells (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cell viability data with ACSS2i treatment, with citation to Li et al., 2021 for comparison to myeloma cells.

claim: ACSS2 inhibitor treatment sensitizes AML cells to AraC treatment.
source: Nonetheless, it was clear that when cells were treated with both drugs, ACSS2i treatment sensitised AML cells to AraC treatment.
evidence: Supported by cell viability assays with combination treatment.

claim: ACSS2 inhibitor reduces the incorporation of acetate to TCA metabolites by approximately 60% after 24 hours of treatment.
source: By performing [2-13C]acetate label incorporation we observed that the ACSS2i reduced the incorporation of acetate to the TCA metabolites by approximately 60% after 24 hr of treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), indicating the incomplete inhibition of the enzyme and thus still accessibility of acetate usage by the cell, providing an explanation for the higher survival in the medium supplemented with acetate compared to control media.
evidence: Supported by tracer-based NMR experiments with ACSS2i treatment.

claim: Acetate confers chemoresistance to AML cells.
source: Our results suggest that acetate confers chemoresistance to AML cells and that the use of ACSS2i sensitizes AML cells to conventional chemotherapies such as AraC.
evidence: Inferred from cell viability experiments showing acetate protection against AraC and sensitization by ACSS2i.

claim: RNA-seq identified 587 differentially expressed genes (q-value <0.1) in MS-5 stromal cells in co-culture compared to alone, with 476 genes upregulated and 111 genes downregulated.
source: With this approach we identified 587 differentially expressed genes (q-value <0.1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B); with 476 genes being upregulated and 111 genes being downregulated in co-culture.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed positive correlation with glycolysis pathway genes and reactive oxygen species pathway genes in MS-5 cells in co-culture.
source: Following clustering of differentially expressed genes, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed (Figure 3A) revealing a positive correlation with the expression of genes that are part of the glycolysis pathway (MSigDB: M5937), as well as the reactive oxygen species pathway (MsigDB: M5938) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Most genes involved in glucose transport and glucose breakdown to pyruvate are upregulated in MS-5 cells in co-culture.
source: Most of the genes involved in glucose transport (Slc2a1 and Slc2a4) and glucose breakdown to pyruvate (Pgm1, Hk2, Gpi1, Pfkl, Gapdh, Pgk1, Pgam1, Pgam2, Eno1, Eno1b, Eno2, and Pkm) were upregulated, including the gene encoding for the 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-biphosphatase 3 (Pfkfb3), a well-known activator of glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes related to pyruvate conversion to acetyl-CoA are downregulated in MS-5 cells in co-culture.
source: In contrast, individual examination of genes related to pyruvate metabolism revealed that the genes related to pyruvate conversion to acetyl-CoA were downregulated (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases (Pdk1, Pdk2, and Pdk4) are upregulated in MS-5 cells in co-culture.
source: Additionally, the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases (Pdk1, Pdk2, and Pdk4), which inhibit the activity of the PDH complex, were found to be upregulated by co-culture (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression analysis and qPCR validation.

claim: Extracellular acetate shows significantly higher 13C label incorporation from [U-13C]glucose in co-culture compared to cell types cultured alone for three AML cell lines.
source: For the three human AML cell lines tested, extracellular acetate presented significantly higher label incorporations from [U-13C]glucose in co-culture compared to cell types cultured alone, providing evidence that the secreted acetate in co-culture derives from glucose.
evidence: Supported by 13C-filtered 1H-NMR experiments with [U-13C]glucose tracer.

claim: Acetate secreted in co-culture derives from glucose.
source: For the three human AML cell lines tested, extracellular acetate presented significantly higher label incorporations from [U-13C]glucose in co-culture compared to cell types cultured alone, providing evidence that the secreted acetate in co-culture derives from glucose.
evidence: Supported by glucose tracer experiments showing label incorporation into acetate.

claim: MS-5 cells show increased intracellular label incorporation from [U-13C]glucose into acetate, alanine, and lactate in co-culture compared to MS-5 alone.
source: Additionally, an increase in labelled acetate, alanine and lactate could be observed intracellularly in MS-5 in co-culture compared to MS-5 alone (Figure 3E). However, only label incorporation in lactate was significant confirming that glycolysis is upregulated in MS-5 cells in co-culture
evidence: Supported by 13C-filtered 1H-NMR experiments on intracellular metabolites.

claim: Acetate secretion in MS-5 cells is not dependent on keto acid dehydrogenases.
source: Moreover, acetate secretion was also observed in MS-5 cells grown in thiamine-free media (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), confirming that the acetate secretion was not dependent on keto acid dehydrogenases (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in thiamine-free media, with citation to Liu et al., 2018 for the role of thiamine in keto acid dehydrogenases.

claim: A non-enzymatic oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate into acetate mediated by ROS has been described in mammalian cells.
source: An alternative mechanism of acetate synthesis involving a non-enzymatic oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate into acetate has previously been described (Liu et al., 2018; Vysochan et al., 2017; Tiziani et al., 2009). This mechanism was reported to be mediated by ROS in mammalian cells and was linked to cells prone to overflow metabolism under the influence of high rates of glycolysis and excess pyruvate.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Liu et al., 2018; Vysochan et al., 2017; Tiziani et al., 2009).

claim: Increasing ROS levels with hydrogen peroxide results in a significant increase in acetate production in SKM-1 and Kasumi-1 co-cultures.
source: Increasing ROS levels with peroxide resulted in a significant increase in acetate production, particularly in SKM-1 and Kasumi-1 cells in co-culture (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by NMR measurements of acetate after H2O2 treatment.

claim: ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine (NAC) decreases acetate levels in both MS-5 cells cultured alone and in all co-cultured cell lines.
source: Additionally, when the ROS scavenger NAC was used, a decrease in the levels of acetate in both MS-5 cells cultured alone and in all the co-cultured cell lines was observed (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by NMR measurements of acetate after NAC treatment.

claim: ROS-scavenging enzyme catalase decreases acetate levels in co-culture.
source: The decrease in acetate levels was additionally confirmed using the ROS-scavenging enzyme, catalase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that acetate synthesis in MS-5 cells in co-culture is mediated by ROS.
evidence: Supported by NMR measurements of acetate after catalase treatment.

claim: Acetate synthesis in MS-5 cells in co-culture is mediated by ROS.
source: The decrease in acetate levels was additionally confirmed using the ROS-scavenging enzyme, catalase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that acetate synthesis in MS-5 cells in co-culture is mediated by ROS.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that ROS scavengers reduce acetate production.

claim: ROS levels in three human AML cell lines are significantly decreased in co-culture compared to cells cultured alone.
source: Our data showed that ROS levels in the three human AML cell lines used were significantly decreased in co-culture, whilst in the stromal cells ROS levels were significantly increased in two of the three co-cultures (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements.

claim: ROS levels in stromal cells are significantly increased in two of three co-cultures with AML cell lines.
source: Our data showed that ROS levels in the three human AML cell lines used were significantly decreased in co-culture, whilst in the stromal cells ROS levels were significantly increased in two of the three co-cultures (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements.

claim: AML cells transfer ROS to stromal cells in co-culture.
source: Our data showed that ROS levels in the three human AML cell lines used were significantly decreased in co-culture, whilst in the stromal cells ROS levels were significantly increased in two of the three co-cultures (Figure 4B). These results suggested that AML cells might transfer ROS to stromal cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AML cells have decreased ROS while stromal cells have increased ROS in co-culture.

claim: Primary AML samples show decreased ROS levels in co-culture and MS-5 cells show increased ROS levels in co-culture for three primary AML samples.
source: Fluorescence analysis showed decreased ROS levels in AML samples in co-culture and increased ROS levels in MS-5 cells in co-culture for the three primary AML samples analysed (Figure 4C), suggesting ROS transfer from AML cells to stromal cells in co-culture.
evidence: Supported by H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements in primary patient samples.

claim: ROS transfer from AML to stromal cells occurs via a contact-dependent mechanism.
source: Fluorescence measurements in both cell types revealed that ROS levels remained unaltered in contact-free co-cultures (Figure 4D), indicating that ROS transfer could only occur via a contact-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurements in permeable membrane co-cultures.

claim: Several gap junction genes including Gja5, Gja8, Gjb5, and Gjc2 are upregulated in MS-5 cells in co-culture.
source: When individually examining the gap junction genes in MS-5 cells cultured alone vs co-culture, we found several gap junction genes upregulated in co-culture such as Gja5, Gja8, Gjb5, and Gjc2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: More than 80% of AML cells from three human AML cell lines incorporate calcein-AM dye from MS-5 cells after three hours of co-culture.
source: We found that, for the three human AML cell lines tested, the percentage of cells that had incorporated the calcein-AM dye from MS-5 cells was larger than 80% (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that AML cells can establish gap junctions with stromal cells when co-cultured in direct contact.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of calcein-AM transfer.

claim: AML cells can establish gap junctions with stromal cells when co-cultured in direct contact.
source: We found that, for the three human AML cell lines tested, the percentage of cells that had incorporated the calcein-AM dye from MS-5 cells was larger than 80% (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that AML cells can establish gap junctions with stromal cells when co-cultured in direct contact.
evidence: Inferred from calcein-AM transfer experiments, which specifically measure gap junction communication.

claim: Carbenoxolone (CBX) treatment significantly reduces calcein-AM fluorescence levels and the percentage of cells with calcein-AM for all human AML cell lines.
source: The CBX treatment significantly reduced fluorescence levels and the percentage of cells with calcein-AM for all the human AML cell lines (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of calcein-AM transfer with CBX treatment.

claim: CBX treatment abrogates the decrease in ROS levels in three human AML cell lines in co-culture.
source: CBX treatment abrogated the decrease in ROS levels in the three human AML cell lines (Figure 5D) and the increase of ROS levels in MS-5 mouse stromal cells (Figure 5E), indicating inhibition of ROS transfer in CBX treated co-cultures.
evidence: Supported by H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements with CBX treatment.

claim: CBX treatment abrogates the increase in ROS levels in MS-5 stromal cells in co-culture.
source: CBX treatment abrogated the decrease in ROS levels in the three human AML cell lines (Figure 5D) and the increase of ROS levels in MS-5 mouse stromal cells (Figure 5E), indicating inhibition of ROS transfer in CBX treated co-cultures.
evidence: Supported by H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements with CBX treatment.

claim: Gap junction inhibition by CBX results in decreased acetate levels in co-cultures of AML and MS-5 cells.
source: We found that inhibition of gap junctions by CBX treatment resulted in a decrease in acetate levels when mouse stromal cells were co-cultured with human AML cell lines compared to untreated co-cultures, indicating that indeed acetate secretion is dependent on the formation of gap junctions between AML and stromal cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by NMR measurements of acetate with CBX treatment.

claim: Acetate secretion is dependent on the formation of gap junctions between AML and stromal cells.
source: We found that inhibition of gap junctions by CBX treatment resulted in a decrease in acetate levels when mouse stromal cells were co-cultured with human AML cell lines compared to untreated co-cultures, indicating that indeed acetate secretion is dependent on the formation of gap junctions between AML and stromal cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that gap junction inhibition reduces acetate secretion.

claim: TBHP treatment accelerates the development of overt AML in MLL-AF9+ transplanted mice, reducing survival.
source: Our results showed that TBHP treatment accelerated the development of overt AML, reducing the survival of the recipient mice, with the number of monocytes in blood five times higher than vehicle-treated leukaemic mice at the end-point analysis (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by in vivo survival analysis and blood monocyte counts.

claim: Combined treatment with TBHP and CBX results in survival and monocyte counts similar to vehicle-injected leukemic mice.
source: In contrast, mice receiving both, TBHP and CBX, displayed survival and monocyte counts similar to vehicle-injected leukaemic mice.
evidence: Supported by in vivo survival analysis and blood monocyte counts.

claim: Gap junction inhibition at least partially reduces the enhancing effect of ROS in the development of AML.
source: These experiments indicate that gap junction inhibition at least partially reduces the enhancing effect of ROS in the development of AML.
evidence: Inferred from in vivo experiments showing that CBX counteracts TBHP effects.

claim: ROS is required for the establishment of gap junctions between AML and stromal cells.
source: We found that, for the three human AML cell lines tested, the calcein-AM transfer was reduced between 50 and 70% compared to cells co-cultured without the ROS scavenger (Figure 5I), indicating that ROS is required for the establishment of gap junctions between AML and stromal cells.
evidence: Supported by calcein-AM transfer experiments with catalase treatment.

claim: ROS transfer from AML cells to stromal cells occurs through gap junctions.
source: Overall, our results indicate that ROS is required for the upregulation of gap junctions facilitating in this way its transfer to stromal cells for acetate production and that inhibition of gap junctions affects acetate secretion by stromal cells (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing gap junction-dependent ROS transfer and acetate production.

claim: AML cells are known to interact and remodel niche cells through secretion of soluble factors, cytokines, or metabolites.
source: AML cells are known to interact and remodel niche cells through various mechanisms, including the secretion of soluble factors, cytokines or metabolites, resulting in a better support of AML cells at the expense of normal haematopoiesis.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: AML cells present abnormally high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: As a consequence of their highly proliferative demand, AML cells (Baccelli et al., 2019; Pollyea et al., 2018; Molina et al., 2018; Lagadinou et al., 2013) and, particularly, chemotherapy-resistant AML cells (Farge et al., 2017) present abnormally high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Li et al., 2011; Hole et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous literature (Baccelli et al., 2019; Pollyea et al., 2018; Molina et al., 2018; Lagadinou et al., 2013; Farge et al., 2017; Li et al., 2011; Hole et al., 2013).

claim: Nestin+ bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells support AML progression by providing glutathione-mediated antioxidant defense.
source: For instance, it was reported that Nestin+ bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) support AML progression by increasing the bioenergetic capacity of AML cells and providing them with glutathione (GSH)-mediated antioxidant defence to balance the excess ROS (Forte et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forte et al., 2020.

claim: Co-culturing BMSCs with AML cells leads to a decrease in AML ROS levels due to activation of the antioxidant enzyme GPx-3.
source: Similarly, a recent study showed that co-culturing BMSCs with AML cells leads to a decrease in AML ROS levels due to an activation of the antioxidant enzyme GPx-3 in AML cells (Vignon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vignon et al., 2020.

claim: Haematopoietic stem cells can transfer ROS to stromal cells via gap junctions to prevent senescence.
source: It has previously reported that haematopoietic stem cells can transfer ROS to stromal cells via gap junction to prevent senescence (Taniguchi Ishikawa et al., 2012), thus, we decided to examine gap junction genes in the transcriptome of MS-5 cultured alone and in co-culture.
evidence: Supported by citation to Taniguchi Ishikawa et al., 2012.

claim: Acetate has been reported as an alternative fuel for cancer cells, especially under low oxygen conditions or lipid depletion.
source: Interestingly, acetate has been reported as an alternative fuel for cancer cells (Lyssiotis and Cantley, 2014; Comerford et al., 2014), especially under low oxygen conditions or lipid depletion (Gao et al., 2016; Schug et al., 2015; Yoshii et al., 2009), but it has not previously been described to participate in crosstalk between any type of cancer cells and their microenvironment.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Lyssiotis and Cantley, 2014; Comerford et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2016; Schug et al., 2015; Yoshii et al., 2009).

claim: Acetate usage to feed the TCA cycle has been described in AML and other types of cancer.
source: Although acetate usage to feed the TCA cycle had already been described in AML (Saborano et al., 2019) and other types of cancer (Schug et al., 2015; Mashimo et al., 2014), this is, to our knowledge, the first report of AML cells utilising acetate secreted by stromal cells in co-culture.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Saborano et al., 2019; Schug et al., 2015; Mashimo et al., 2014).

claim: This is the first report of AML cells utilizing acetate secreted by stromal cells in co-culture.
source: Although acetate usage to feed the TCA cycle had already been described in AML (Saborano et al., 2019) and other types of cancer (Schug et al., 2015; Mashimo et al., 2014), this is, to our knowledge, the first report of AML cells utilising acetate secreted by stromal cells in co-culture.
evidence: Authors' claim of novelty based on comparison to existing literature.

claim: Enrichment of hypoxia genes and elevated Pdk expression have been reported to be related to higher glycolytic activity.
source: Enrichment of hypoxia genes and elevated Pdk expression have been reported to be related to higher glycolytic activity (Testa et al., 2016; Kocabas et al., 2015; Takubo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Testa et al., 2016; Kocabas et al., 2015; Takubo et al., 2013).

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic data of stroma cells in vivo has shown three specific clusters with upregulated glycolysis and hypoxia pathways.
source: Additionally, published single-cell transcriptomic data of stroma cells in vivo by the group of Scadden, has shown three specific clusters which have upregulated glycolysis and hypoxia pathways (Baryawno et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baryawno et al., 2019.

claim: The osteoprogenitor cluster was shown to be upregulated in leukemic mice and shared the same hallmark gene sets as MS-5 in co-culture.
source: In particular, the osteoprogenitor cluster was shown to be upregulated in leukaemic mice and shared the same hallmark gene sets that MS-5 in co-culture (TNFα, Hypoxia, allograft rejection, glycolysis, IFNγ, K-RAS, complement, epithelial to mesenchymal transition and IL2-STAT5) (Baryawno et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baryawno et al., 2019 and comparison to current study's GSEA results.

claim: Other cancer cells have been shown to modulate stromal metabolism by increasing glycolysis.
source: Similarly, other cancer cells Shan et al., 2017; Migneco et al., 2010; Pavlides et al., 2009; Cruz-Bermúdez et al., 2019 have also been shown to modulate stromal metabolism by increasing glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Shan et al., 2017; Migneco et al., 2010; Pavlides et al., 2009; Cruz-Bermúdez et al., 2019).

claim: AML cells in co-culture present lower levels of ROS than AML cells cultured alone, which is in agreement with recent studies in primary AML and mesenchymal stromal cell co-cultures.
source: However, our data has shown that AML cells in co-culture present lower levels of ROS than AML cells cultured alone, which is in agreement with recent studies in primary AML and mesenchymal stromal cell co-cultures (Forte et al., 2020; Vignon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by current study's data and citations to Forte et al., 2020 and Vignon et al., 2020.

claim: Current mechanisms to describe decreased ROS in AML cells in co-culture involve mitochondrial transfer and activation of glutathione-related antioxidant pathways.
source: The current mechanisms to describe this phenomenon involve mitochondrial transfer and activation of glutathione-related antioxidant pathways (Forte et al., 2020; Vignon et al., 2020), although previous data on haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) revealed that HSCs can directly transfer ROS via gap junctions to stromal cells (Taniguchi Ishikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Forte et al., 2020; Vignon et al., 2020; Taniguchi Ishikawa et al., 2012).

claim: Targeting ROS transfer via modulation of gap junctions to suppress acetate provision by stromal cells or targeting acetate usage could serve as an adjuvant therapy to eradicate AML.
source: Targeting ROS transfer via modulation of gap junctions to suppress acetate provision by stromal cells or targeting acetate usage could serve as an adjuvant therapy to eradicate AML.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on the study's findings.

claim: Co-culture of AML and stromal cells results in higher glucose consumption and lactate secretion compared to single cultures.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, higher consumption of glucose along with a higher secretion of lactate was observed in AML and stromal cells in co-culture compared to single cultures, suggesting a higher glycolytic flux in co-culture.
evidence: Supported by NMR measurements of extracellular metabolites.

claim: The overall increase in glycolysis in co-culture is a result of culturing both cell types together rather than a synergistic effect.
source: However, the levels of glucose consumption and lactate production in co-culture were similar to the sum of the glucose consumption and lactate production levels of the AML and stromal cells in single cultures, suggesting that the overall increase in glycolysis in co-culture was just a result of culturing both cell types together.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of metabolite levels in co-culture vs. sum of individual cultures.

claim: AML cell lines do not show differences in proliferation rates when cultured alone vs. in co-culture over 48 hours.
source: Over 48 hr, none of the human AML cell lines tested presented differences in their proliferation rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), thus confirming that the metabolic changes found in co-culture were caused by a mechanism independent of changes in proliferation.
evidence: Supported by CFSE proliferation assay data.

claim: Metabolic changes found in co-culture are caused by a mechanism independent of changes in proliferation.
source: Over 48 hr, none of the human AML cell lines tested presented differences in their proliferation rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), thus confirming that the metabolic changes found in co-culture were caused by a mechanism independent of changes in proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from proliferation assay showing no differences in growth rates.

claim: Acetylcarnitine is produced by cells when large amounts of acetyl-CoA are present in the mitochondria.
source: Acetylcarnitine is known to be produced by cells when large amounts of acetyl-CoA are present in the mitochondria (Childress et al., 1967; Stephens et al., 2007), which could be in line with this experiment in which a high concentration of [2-13C]acetate (4 mM) was used.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Childress et al., 1967; Stephens et al., 2007).

claim: MS-5 is a stromal mouse cell line capable of maintaining haematopoiesis.
source: For this purpose, three human AML cell lines (SKM-1, Kasumi-1 and HL-60) representing different AML subtypes (M5, M2 t(8;21), and M2, respectively) were cultured separately and in co-culture with MS-5, a stromal mouse cell line capable of maintaining haematopoiesis (Itoh et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Itoh et al., 1989.

claim: AML cells interact and modulate components of their surrounding microenvironment for their own benefit.
source: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) cells interact and modulate components of their surrounding microenvironment into their own benefit.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Stromal cells have been shown to support AML survival and progression through various mechanisms.
source: Stromal cells have been shown to support AML survival and progression through various mechanisms.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: AML cells show a highly adaptive metabolism that allows them to efficiently use a variety of nutrients to obtain energy and generate biomass.
source: AML cells show a highly adaptive metabolism that allows them to efficiently use a variety of nutrients to obtain energy and generate biomass (reviewed in Kreitz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Kreitz et al., 2019.

claim: High metabolic plasticity confers AML cells a strong advantage against normal haematopoietic cells and has been related to AML aggressiveness.
source: This high metabolic plasticity confers AML cells a strong advantage against normal haematopoietic cells and has been related to AML aggressiveness.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Adipocytes in the niche secrete fatty acids which are metabolized by AML cells through β-oxidation to obtain energy, protecting AML cells from apoptosis and ROS.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that adipocytes in the niche secrete fatty acids, which are metabolised by AML cells through β-oxidation to obtain energy, protecting AML cells from apoptosis and ROS (Shafat et al., 2017; Tabe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shafat et al., 2017 and Tabe et al., 2017.
